source: Chen, Zuo, Cai, Yin, Zhang (2024) Towards controllable generative design: FBS ontology plus LLMs (J Mech Des 146(12), accepted manuscript PDF)
finding: Full text read this session (earlier b26 saw only the abstract). FBS is used as a three-stage prompt chain on ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125): requirements to function ('What functions should a [RQM] have?'), function to behaviour ('What kind of design can afford [FCN]?'), behaviour to structure ('What design structures can achieve [BEH]?'). At each stage the human picks words from the output that feed the next template. The picked function-structure pairs are shown as stimuli for sketching a leg rehabilitation device.
numbers: 80 participants, 4 groups of 20 (each 15 novices with 3-4 years of design education plus 5 professionals with over 8 years). G2 = FBS chain. G1 = fixed prompts from a fine-tuned model (Zhu and Luo). G3 = free prompting of ChatGPT. G4 = Google search only, no AI. 30 minutes per person. 80 sketches mixed, 3 experts with 10 years of experience scored each against a benchmark concept on 5 criteria (novelty, feasibility, usability, functionality, cost).
limits: Human-in-the-loop: people choose which words go forward, so the model alone is not tested. Conditions differ in more than FBS structure (G1 uses a different model and prompts). No token or time-on-LLM control. Authors test their own method.
agent_relevance: Closest thing found to a test of F-to-Be-to-S staging against plain prompting, but with a human selector at each hop. An agent version would need the selection step done by code or a judge.

source: Chen, Zuo, Cai, Yin, Zhang (2024) Towards controllable generative design: FBS ontology plus LLMs (J Mech Des 146(12), accepted manuscript PDF) results
finding: The FBS chain group scored highest overall. Weighted concept score: G2 FBS 3.31 (SD 0.58), G1 fixed-form 2.94 (SD 0.55), G3 free prompting 2.90 (SD 0.47), G4 no AI 2.63 (SD 0.53). One-way ANOVA F about 15.99, p about 1.7e-9. t-tests: G2 vs G1 t 3.18 p 0.0019; G2 vs G3 t 4.22 p 4.8e-5; G2 vs G4 t 6.64; G1 vs G4 t -3.24; G3 vs G4 t -2.90. Fleiss kappa among raters 0.66 on the average score (0.63 to 0.79 per criterion).
numbers: Per-criterion group means (novice/professional) for G2: novelty 3.53/3.60, feasibility 3.64/3.53, usability 3.58/3.00, functionality 3.26/3.20, cost 3.15/3.40. Base concept scored 3.0 on each. Gain of G2 over G3 is 0.41 points on a 5-point scale.
limits: Benchmark-relative scoring, so the numbers are not absolute quality. Single task (a rehabilitation device) and one model.
agent_relevance: Sign is consistent with FBS staging helping over free prompting; size (about 0.4 on 5 points, one task) is modest.

source: Chen, Zuo, Cai, Yin, Zhang (2024) Towards controllable generative design: FBS ontology plus LLMs (J Mech Des 146(12), accepted manuscript PDF) statistical and expertise notes
finding: Back-of-envelope check: with 20 concepts per group and SD about 0.55, a G2 vs G4 gap of 0.68 gives t near 3.9, not the reported 6.64. A t of 6.64 matches about 60 scores per group, which suggests the tests used per-rater scores (3 raters x 20 concepts) as independent units. That would inflate significance. Expertise: G2 improved novices by 0.51 over G1 and 0.68 over G3, but professionals by only 0.37 and 0.02. Novices in G2 scored 0.08 above professionals.
numbers: Novice average G2 3.43 vs professional 3.35 (n 15 and 5). Professionals: G2 3.35, G1 2.98, G3 3.33. So against free prompting, FBS gave professionals about no gain (0.02).
limits: The pseudoreplication reading is my calculation from the printed table, not stated by the authors. Professional n is 5 per group.
agent_relevance: A scaffold may help weaker reasoners more than strong ones; this fits the idea that a scaffold's gain shrinks as the base reasoner gets better. Treat the p-values as overstated.

source: Gero, Kannengiesser, Crilly (2022) Abstracting and formalising the design co-evolution model (Design Science 8:e14)
finding: Defines co-evolution formally as reciprocal exogenous change between categories (a change in one category triggered by the other, then the reverse). Illustrates it on one FBS-coded protocol. Problem space = R, F, Be issues; solution space = Bs, S, D issues. A change is counted at the first occurrence of a new F, B or S issue (a 'first occurrence' code).
numbers: Data: one 1-hour session, a team of 3 professional engineers designing a personal entertainment system, taken from 19 sessions (Milovanovic, Gero and Becker 2021). FBS coding by two independent coders; first-occurrence coding by one coder, semi-automatic string matching plus manual synonym check.
limits: Illustration only. One session, no inferential statistics, no held-out check. Influence is coded syntactically: if one first occurrence follows another, the first is taken to have influenced it.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap code-measurable signal for an agent trace: count first occurrences of new F, B, S items and whether problem and solution items trigger each other.

source: Gero, Kannengiesser, Crilly (2022) co-evolution: problem/solution and designer-level illustrations
finding: Counting attention switches between problem and solution overstates co-evolution. In illustration 1 the switch count overestimated co-evolution episodes by almost 50%. In illustration 2 (designers X, Y, Z as categories) turn-taking overestimated by about 100%. Designer Y spoke about half as many segments as X and Z but drove more co-evolution than that share implies: 35 exogenous changes with Z versus 29 for X with Z.
numbers: Co-evolution came in spurts and continued near the end of the session. Isolated one-way exogenous changes (around segments 241 and 261) are not co-evolution on their own.
limits: Single protocol; the percentages come from one session.
agent_relevance: Supports measuring idea-to-idea influence, not mode switching, when judging whether an agent really revises its problem framing.

source: Gero, Kannengiesser, Crilly (2022) co-evolution: function, behaviour, structure illustration and system 1
finding: With F, B and S as three categories, most co-evolution was between behaviour and structure and was almost continuous through the session. Function-involving co-evolution was mostly in the first half, and mostly with behaviour, not structure. The authors read the scarcity of function-structure co-evolution as few system 1 (intuition) episodes; system 2 runs F to Be to S, system 1 goes F to S directly.
numbers: No counts printed for this illustration; shown as cumulative curves (Figure 8).
limits: Descriptive only, one team. The system 1 reading is an interpretation by the authors, not a test.
agent_relevance: Behaviour is the hinge state: expected behaviour (analysis, evaluation) is where most of the exchange happens. Suggests S-states should keep a behaviour slot active throughout.

source: Gero, Kannengiesser, Crilly (2022) literature review of Maher and Poon (1996) co-evolution model
finding: Describes Maher and Poon (1996) as a co-evolutionary genetic algorithm with two populations, a problem space P and a solution space S, each changing over time and influencing the other (P to P and S to S = evolution; S to P and P to S = exogenous). Quality is the fitness of the current P-S pair; low fitness makes both searches refocus. The model began as an algorithm for computer creative design, then was reused to describe historic projects (Poon and Maher 1997) and human lab designers (Dorst and Cross 2001; Maher and Tang 2003). Later uses: professional teams (Wiltschnig et al. 2013), education.
numbers: No experimental numbers for Maher and Poon in this source. It gives no replication figures.
limits: Secondary account. The 1996 paper itself and Maher's case-based design work were not available: no free full text could be fetched.
agent_relevance: The algorithmic form (two populations plus a fitness check that triggers refocus) maps to an agent loop: propose, score fit between current problem statement and current solution, reframe when fit is low.

source: Kannengiesser and Gero (2019) Design thinking, fast and slow (Design Science), full text read
finding: The Design Science paper is a framework paper. It has no labelled hypotheses H1 or H2, no participants and no statistics. It only says the framework allows empirically testing whether system 1 and 2 thinking occur in design, and that initial protocol results from professional engineers and students confirm the model. That empirical test is a separate paper: Kannengiesser and Gero (2019), 'Empirical evidence for Kahneman's system 1 and system 2 thinking in design', Human Behavior in Design pp 89-100.
numbers: None for the hypotheses. It cites FBS coding of over 10,000 hours of designing in aerospace work.
limits: Page text read through a summariser in two chunks (first 100,000 characters). The conference paper's host (par.nsf.gov) refused connection, so H1/H2 results were not obtained.
agent_relevance: Do not cite any H2 outcome. Whether professionals use more system 1 than students stays unknown here.

source: Dunivin (2024) Scalable qualitative coding with LLMs: chain-of-thought reasoning matches human performance in some hermeneutic tasks (arXiv 2401.15170)
finding: Not about FBS but the nearest held-out reliability test for LLM coding with an ambiguous codebook. GPT-4 reached substantial agreement (kappa 0.6 or more) with a human gold standard for 8 of 9 codes and excellent (0.79 or more) for 3. GPT-3.5 did badly (mean 0.34, max 0.55). Prompting the model to give a rationale before the code raised agreement.
numbers: 111 gold-standard passages, 9 codes. GPT-4 per-code: mean kappa 0.68 with rationale vs 0.59 without. GPT-4 full-codebook in one prompt: 0.60 vs 0.46. GPT-3.5: 0.34 vs 0.29. Per-code prompting beat full codebook (0.68 vs 0.60). Hardest codes had few cases (Coalition Building n=9: 0.60; Out of the Mouth of Activists n=11: 0.30).
quote: coding fidelity improves considerably when the LLM is prompted to give rationale justifying its coding decisions
limits: Sociology passages about one historical figure, not design protocols. Kappa on rare codes is unstable. Codebook was tuned on a training set before the gold test.
agent_relevance: If FBS coding is automated, code one label per call with a rationale, and expect weak reliability on rare or fuzzy labels (behaviour).

finding: Model rationales exposed ambiguous code definitions; rewording a definition sometimes fixed the targeted passages but broke others that were previously right. This is the same ambiguity that Sahadevan 2024 met when sorting F, Be, Bs.
numbers: 232 passages extracted automatically, 111 used as gold. Revision cycles were done on a training set.
limits: Process description by the author, not a controlled study.
agent_relevance: An FBS tag check should be tested on a held-out set after any rewording of tag definitions, since fixes can regress other items.

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2024) Exploring the capabilities of LLMs for generating diverse design solutions: parameter and prompt details (arXiv 2405.02345)
finding: Re-read for the seed and variance gap. Diversity of GPT-4 output across decoding settings showed no monotonic trend with temperature or top-P. Best LLM setting was temperature 1 and top-P 1 (the API default). Temperature 2 with top-P 1 gave incoherent text and was dropped. Two separate sets of 50 human solutions served as a noise floor; LLM sets scored below both, e.g. -24% DPP at temperature 0 and top-P 0 in the froth topic.
numbers: Four diversity metrics (DPP, nearest sample, convex hull, distance to centroid) agreed (mostly strong positive Spearman correlations). Critique-critique (one extra edit pass over 50 solutions) gave the biggest rise; a persona line 'excellent at ideating far-fetched ideas' also helped; 'unique' scored below 'creative' and 'novel'. Logistic regression on embeddings: LLM class recall 1.00 in all five topics; human class recall 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.80 by topic.
limits: No FBS reformulation step and no test across random seeds as such; only parameter grids and prompt styles. Single model.
agent_relevance: No evidence that an FBS reformulation restores spread. What worked here was an edit pass and a persona line, both cheap.

source: Elhambakhsh, Grandi, Ko (2025) domain adaptation of LLMs for classifying mechanical assembly components: replication search
finding: No second study that repeats the finding that function-classification test accuracy falls as fine-tuning data grows was found. The search APIs (arXiv, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex) were all rate-limited in this run and the web search budget ran out, so absence is weak evidence.
numbers: None new. See a20 and c06 for the original figures.
limits: This line records a failed search; the URL points to the original paper only.
agent_relevance: Keep K08's note that the falling test accuracy is probably a fine-tuning artefact.

source: AI- and ontology-based enhancements to FMEA (arXiv 2511.17743) claim about FBS and conceptual errors
finding: This review says embedding FBS reasoning in ontologies lets designers align intent with constraints and reduce conceptual errors in early modelling, citing Eisenbart and Gericke 2020. It gives no measurement of errors with and without an FBS evaluation step.
limits: Narrative review, claim is secondhand. Eisenbart and Gericke 2020 was not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat 'FBS evaluation steps reduce errors in LLM loops' as untested.

source: Search record for gap 1: FBS-tagged reasoning vs plain chain of thought at equal tokens
finding: Web searches for FBS ontology plus LLM agent or prompting surfaced Chen 2024 (human-in-loop), Sahadevan 2024 (classification), a CEUR agent ontology paper (kgmdse paper6, proposal only) and the FMEA review. None compares F/Be/Bs/S labelled agent reasoning with plain chain of thought at equal token budget.
limits: Limited by search budget (3 queries on this topic, then the budget ran out; arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs returned HTTP 429). Absence is not proof.
agent_relevance: The equal-token test is still ours to run.

source: Search record for gaps 5 and 6: decomposition-recomposition forced by prompt; expected vs derived behaviour check in LLM design loops
finding: No paper found that forces expert-style decomposition-recomposition on an LLM, nor one that ablates an expected-versus-derived behaviour check in an LLM design loop. Closest: Zhang et al. 2025 (zero-shot chain of thought imitating problem-driven and solution-driven designers; c20) and the Ma 2024 critique pass (c09, c10).
agent_relevance: Both remain open; the critique pass is the only measured analogue of an evaluation step.

source: Search snippets on LLM qualitative coding reliability (arXiv 2507.14384, 2508.14764; JMIR 2024 e59050)
finding: Snippets only: task decomposition into steps reached kappa 0.744 on a policy classification task; GPT-4o and GPT-4.5-preview reached kappa above 0.6 on three of four themes after prompt tuning. Consistent with Dunivin, but not read.
limits: Not opened; secondhand from a search summary; none use design protocols.
agent_relevance: Weak support that structured multi-step coding can reach usable kappa. No FBS-specific multi-coder kappa exists yet (gap 2 open).

source: Gero (1990) Design prototypes and Gero and Kannengiesser (2004) situated FBS: access attempt
finding: The AAAI page returned an access-denied bot page. The Springer chapter for 2004 was not reachable either. No numbers were obtained. The only causal-test information is indirect: the 2022 and 2019 papers show the eight processes used as coding categories, not manipulated.
limits: Gap 3 unresolved except for that indirect point.
agent_relevance: Do not claim any causal test of the eight processes.

source: Search record for gap 4: Maher and Poon 1996 results and replications
finding: Search found only secondary descriptions of Maher and Poon (1996) and a companion, Poon and Maher (1996) 'Emergent behaviour in co-evolutionary design' (AI in Design 96). Dorst and Cross (2001) and Maher and Tang (2003) are named as human-protocol follow-ups; their numbers were not retrieved (Springer and Cambridge page fetches returned 404).
limits: Gap 4 only partly closed: model description yes, numbers and replications no.
agent_relevance: Use the co-evolution model as a design pattern, not as a replicated empirical finding.
